content: Positive airway pressure (PAP) is a respiratory ventilation technique primarily used to treat sleep apnea. It was initially developed for this purpose but is also commonly employed in critically ill patients with respiratory failure and in neonates. PAP ventilation can help avoid the need for endotracheal intubation or facilitate earlier extubation in these patients. A Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machine is predominantly used by patients at home to manage sleep apnea. Obstructive sleep apnea occurs when the upper airway narrows due to muscle relaxation during sleep, leading to reduced oxygen levels in the blood and sleep disturbances. The CPAP machine prevents this by delivering a stream of compressed air through a nasal pillow, nose mask, or full-face mask. This air pressure keeps the airway open, enabling unobstructed breathing and reducing or preventing apneas and hypopneas. Additionally, CPAP therapy often eliminates or reduces snoring. The CPAP machine delivers air at a prescribed pressure, known as the titrated pressure, which is determined by a sleep physician after reviewing a polysomnography study conducted in a sleep laboratory. The titrated pressure is the level at which most, if not all, apneas and hypopneas are prevented. This pressure is measured in centimeters of water (cm H₂O), with most patients requiring pressures between 6 and 14 cm H₂O. Standard CPAP machines can deliver pressures ranging from 4 to 20 cm H₂O, while specialized units can go up to 25 or 30 cm H₂O. CPAP therapy is highly effective for treating obstructive sleep apnea, and some patients notice significant improvements in sleep quality and overall quality of life after just one night of use. However, many prospective CPAP users are hesitant to start therapy due to the perceived discomfort of the nose mask and hose, as well as the vigorous airflow required for some patients. While some individuals adapt to the treatment within weeks, others struggle for longer periods or discontinue therapy altogether. Patient compliance can be improved with support from durable medical equipment (DME) providers, who often allow patients to choose from a variety of PAP devices and masks. PAP manufacturers offer different models at various price points, and masks come in multiple sizes and shapes, requiring some users to try several options before finding a suitable fit. The CPAP system was first developed in 1981 by Professor Colin Sullivan at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital. There are several types of PAP devices: Fixed-pressure CPAP delivers a constant pressure to the patient. APAP (Automatic Positive Airway Pressure) adjusts the pressure automatically on a breath-by-breath basis, providing the minimum pressure needed to maintain an open airway by measuring resistance in the patient’s breathing. VPAP™ or BiPAP® (Variable/Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure) provides two pressure levels: a higher pressure for inhalation (IPAP) and a lower pressure for exhalation (EPAP). xPAP ST (Spontaneous Time) machines enforce a set number of breaths per minute and are used for patients with central apneas. PAP machines consist of three main components: 1. A flow generator (the PAP machine) that provides compressed air. 2. A hose that connects the flow generator to the interface, sometimes via a humidifier. 3. An interface (mask) that connects to the user’s airway. Optional features include: Humidifiers to add moisture to the air, which can be heated or passive. Heated humidifiers use a water chamber to eliminate dryness, with adjustable temperatures. Passive humidifiers rely on ambient air temperature and are less effective but still improve comfort. Ramp features temporarily lower the pressure to help users fall asleep more easily, gradually increasing to the prescribed level. Exhalation pressure relief reduces pressure during exhalation to decrease the effort required, known as C-Flex® in Respironics machines or EPR™ in ResMed devices. Flexible chin straps help prevent mouth breathing, maintaining a closed pressure system while allowing the patient to open their mouth if needed. Data logging records compliance and detailed event data, enabling sleep physicians or patients to analyze treatment effectiveness. This feature enhances PAP tolerance and compliance. Proper care and maintenance are essential for PAP machines to function correctly, ensure longevity, and maintain patient comfort. Maintenance requirements vary by machine type and usage conditions and are detailed in the manufacturer’s instruction manual. Weekly maintenance is typically recommended, including checking for wear and tear, cleaning filters, and replacing them as needed. Hoses and masks should be cleaned regularly to prevent the accumulation of skin particles, particulate matter, and mold. Humidification units must be kept free of mold and algae. Electrical components should be inspected for damage to avoid shock or fire hazards. Cleaning should be done without immersing the unit in water. Portability is crucial for patients who travel, as continuous compliance is vital for treatment success. Modern PAP units are becoming lighter and more compact, often with carrying cases. Many units have dual-voltage power supplies for international use. Air travel considerations include compatibility with aircraft power supplies and altitude adjustments. Some patients also use supplemental oxygen, which may present fire risks and restrictions, especially with bottled gas. However, oxygen concentrators are increasingly permitted on airlines. In many countries, PAP machines require a prescription, and treatment typically begins after a sleep study in an accredited sleep lab. A physician, often a specialist in respiratory medicine, ENT, or neurology, interprets the sleep study results and estimates the appropriate pressure settings. These settings are later confirmed during a follow-up sleep study with the CPAP mask in use. In the United States, PAP machines are available online at discounted prices, but patients must handle insurance reimbursement themselves. Some government programs may cover the cost of PAP devices. In the United Kingdom, PAP machines are available through the National Health Service or privately with a prescription. In Australia, PAP machines can be purchased without a prescription, though some suppliers require a referral. Low-income earners may access free or low-cost machines through state health programs, and private health insurance may offer partial rebates. In hospital settings, PAP ventilation is often used for patients with acute type 1 or type 2 respiratory failure. It is typically reserved for cases where oxygen delivered via a face mask is insufficient or harmful. Patients on PAP ventilation are closely monitored in intensive care or specialized respiratory units. Common conditions treated with PAP in hospitals include congestive heart failure and acute exacerbations of obstructive airway diseases like COPD and asthma. PAP is not used in cases of compromised airways or impaired consciousness. Hospital PAP therapy differs from home use, as it focuses on improving gas exchange in the lungs and reducing the work of breathing. During inspiration, the inspiratory positive airway pressure (IPAP) forces air into the lungs, reducing the effort required by respiratory muscles. It also prevents the collapse of bronchioles and alveoli at the end of expiration, reducing the pressure needed to reopen them. This process, called recruitment, improves ventilation/perfusion matching and increases the functional residual capacity, making breathing more efficient.
